1030.title: Soviet Jewry
1030.hook: Jews in the Soviet Union are denied the right to practice or to leave
1030.howItsDone: Jews retell the story of the refuseniks alongside the Exodus, and 'Let my people go' from Exodus 5:1 became the slogan of the worldwide movement for Soviet Jewry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, airlifts, and your line: on eagles' wings. A new week begins somewhere very different, behind a closed border.

Someone keeps an ear on the stairwell. In a kitchen in Moscow, late at night, curtains drawn, a handful of people lean over one worn Hebrew textbook, its pages typed and retyped and passed from hand to hand. Teaching Hebrew like this could cost a person their job, or worse. Every person at this table has asked the government for permission to leave for Israel, and every one has been told no. They have a name for themselves: refuseniks.
screen: `A KITCHEN IN MOSCOW, CURTAINS DRAWN.` → `ONE WORN HEBREW BOOK.` → `EVERY ONE TOLD NO.`

segments.voice: In the Soviet Union, religion was officially discouraged, and Jewish life was squeezed hard. Synagogues were few and watched. Hebrew was difficult to learn. Jews often met suspicion at universities and at work. And for a long time, few were allowed to leave. Then some Jews began to apply anyway, to emigrate to Israel. Applications were refused, sometimes with a vague reason about state secrets, and the person who asked could lose their job just for asking. That's a refusenik: someone refused permission to leave. Some waited for years. Inside, they did what Jews had done under pressure before: learned in secret, taught each other Hebrew, kept the holidays quietly. On Simchat Torah, young Jews gathered outside a Moscow synagogue and danced in the street. Outside the country, Jews and non-Jews around the world took up their cause, with a slogan from Exodus. Moses and Aaron stand before Pharaoh and say: "Let My people go, that they may hold a feast unto Me in the wilderness." Notice the second half, the part a slogan can leave off. The demand isn't only to leave. It's to be free to worship, to hold the feast: freedom to go, and freedom to be who you are where you stand. In time, the gates opened, and families left, some to Israel, some to America and elsewhere. Tomorrow, one refusenik who found a way to stay free inside a prison cell.
screen: `JEWISH LIFE SQUEEZED HARD.` · `REFUSED, AND PUNISHED FOR ASKING.` · `HEBREW IN SECRET KITCHENS.` · `LET MY PEOPLE GO, TO HOLD A FEAST.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're free to do that someone, somewhere, is not: read a book of your choosing, learn a word of Hebrew, light a candle, say a blessing out loud, sit in silence without anyone checking. Choose one and do it now, slowly and on purpose, remembering the kitchens where it cost something. If you pray, you can do it as a prayer.
Refusenik. A Soviet Jew refused permission to leave, often punished for asking, who kept Jewish life going in secret.
Your line: let my people go. Some waited years to hear yes. Day one thousand thirty, done.

1031.title: Natan Sharansky
1031.hook: a refusenik imprisoned for years, then freed
1031.howItsDone: Psalm 23 is said by Jews at the third Sabbath meal and in times of fear and mourning, and Sharansky's story is retold as part of the history of the movement for Soviet Jewry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, refusenik, and your line: let my people go. Today, one refusenik, and a prison cell.

The last order the guards give him is simple: walk straight across the bridge, to the car on the other side. It's a cold morning on the edge of Berlin, and he stands at one end. He has spent years in Soviet prisons doing what he was told, or refusing to. He sets off across the bridge, and he walks in a zigzag. A tiny act. By his own account, it was on purpose. His name is Natan Sharansky.
screen: `A BRIDGE IN BERLIN.` → `WALK STRAIGHT.` → `HE WALKS IN A ZIGZAG.`

segments.voice: He was called Anatoly then, a young mathematician in Moscow who loved chess. He applied to emigrate to Israel and was refused. He became a refusenik, and then a voice for others, meeting foreign reporters and speaking up for human rights. He was arrested and accused of spying, a charge he denied and his supporters called false. He spent years in prisons and labor camps, including long stretches in punishment cells, cold and alone. Meanwhile his wife, Avital, already in Israel, traveled from country to country saying his name to anyone who would listen. What kept him going inside? He has written that the guards could control his body but not his inner world. He played chess games in his head. And he had a small book of Psalms that reached him from Avital. When guards took it away, he fought to get it back. Years later he called his memoir by a line from that book: Fear No Evil. It comes from Psalm 23: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, For Thou art with me." A cell can hold a body. In his telling, it never held his choices: what to think about, what to refuse, what to keep. The zigzag on the bridge was one more of them, made in plain sight of the guards.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place in your life that feels like a small cell: a job you can't leave yet, an illness, a family tangle, a long wait. Don't fight it for now; just find one thing inside it that is still yours, your breath, your kindness, a line you choose to remember, the way you answer, and hold it. If you pray, you can say the psalm's words: I will fear no evil.
Natan Sharansky. A refusenik imprisoned for years in the Soviet Union, who held on to his book of Psalms and walked to freedom in a zigzag.
Your line: free inside. Even a walk across a bridge can be a choice. Until tomorrow.

1032.title: Heschel at Selma (1965)
1032.hook: Abraham Joshua Heschel marches with Martin Luther King and calls it a kind of prayer
1032.howItsDone: Heschel's march at Selma is retold in synagogues and Jewish schools, often around Martin Luther King Jr. Day, as an example of prayer joined to action for justice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Natan Sharansky, and your line: free inside. Today, a different kind of walk, in Alabama.

Arms linked, a long column of marchers sets out along the highway from Selma, Alabama, for Montgomery, to demand the right to vote. In the front row, a few places from Martin Luther King Jr., walks a man with a white beard and a cap, in a coat and tie, a garland of flowers around his neck. He is Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel, a scholar who spent his life writing about prayer. When he got home, he said this march had been a kind of prayer too.
screen: `A HIGHWAY OUT OF SELMA.` → `ARMS LINKED, NEAR THE FRONT.` → `A KIND OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Heschel came from a family of Hasidic rabbis in Poland and got out of Europe before the war. Much of his family did not. In America he taught and wrote about prayer, the Sabbath, and the prophets. The prophets fascinated him because they couldn't stay quiet when someone was being crushed. In Selma, Black Americans had been beaten for trying to register to vote, and marchers had already been attacked on a bridge out of town. King called on clergy to come. Heschel came. Afterward, he wrote that he felt as if his legs were praying. For him, prayer wasn't only words read from a book. It could be a whole body moving toward justice. The prophet Amos talks this way. Speaking for God to people who trample the poor, he says their feasts and the noise of their songs are not wanted, and then: "But let justice well up as waters, And righteousness as a mighty stream." King used that line too, in his own wording, from pulpits and podiums. Two men from two traditions, walking in step, carrying the same prophet. This doesn't mean marching replaces praying; Heschel kept praying in the synagogue. It means the wall between the two can be thin. A walk can begin with a prayer.
screen: `A RABBI WHO WROTE ABOUT PRAYER.` · `SELMA: THE RIGHT TO VOTE.` · `MY LEGS WERE PRAYING.` · `LET JUSTICE WELL UP AS WATERS.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and take a slow walk, across the room or down a hall; if walking isn't possible, let your hands or your breath keep a slow, steady beat. As you move, bring to mind one cause you care about, or one person who needs justice, and let each step, or each breath, be for them. If you pray, let the walking be your prayer.
Heschel. The rabbi who marched with Martin Luther King Jr. at Selma for the right to vote, and said afterward that his legs were praying.
Your line: marching as prayer. And a prayer can end with your feet. That's day one thousand thirty-two.

1033.title: Civil rights
1033.hook: Jews were among those who joined the American civil rights movement
1033.howItsDone: Jewish communities remember the civil rights movement through the Torah's command not to stand idly by a neighbor's blood, and some synagogues hold joint services with Black churches around Martin Luther King Jr. Day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Heschel, and your line: marching as prayer. Today, the wider movement Heschel walked into.

Three young civil rights workers drive out, one summer day in Mississippi, to look at a Black church that has been burned. They never come back. Days go by. Their car is found in a swamp, burned too. James Chaney was a Black Mississippian. Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner were young Jewish men from New York. All three were murdered by Klansmen. Their names are said together, and they belong together.
screen: `A SUMMER IN MISSISSIPPI.` → `THREE WHO NEVER CAME BACK.` → `CHANEY, GOODMAN, SCHWERNER.`

segments.voice: The civil rights movement was led by Black Americans: preachers, students, sharecroppers, mothers, who faced its dangers every day. Others came to stand with them, and Jews were among those who came. Some went south as volunteers to register voters. A group of rabbis was arrested in Florida for joining a protest. Lawyers took cases; donors paid for bail. Why did they come? Some pointed to memory. At every Passover, Jews tell the story of slavery in Egypt as their own, and the Torah says it plainly: "thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt." Black churches had long sung the Exodus as their own story too, so the two communities shared a song. Others pointed to the verse from Leviticus that came up with never again: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD." Here, not standing idly by meant going. And the honest part: it was not a simple story. Some Southern Jews were afraid to speak up, and some agreed with segregation. In later years, real tensions grew between some Black and Jewish leaders, alongside real friendships that lasted. So this isn't a trophy for anyone's shelf. It's a record of people who chose not to stand idly by, and of the people who led them. Justice for all is a phrase Americans say about their own country. The movement asked the country to mean it.
screen: `LED BY BLACK AMERICANS.` · `JEWS AMONG THOSE WHO CAME.` · `REMEMBER YOU WERE A SLAVE.` · `NOT A SIMPLE STORY.` · then, large: `STAND NOT IDLY BY.`

segments.voice: Go back to the car on that summer road, driving toward a church that had been burned, and think of what it takes to go toward a place like that, not away from it. Then think of someone who stood up for another person's rights, famous or not, a teacher, a grandparent, a neighbor, and hold their face for a while.
Civil rights. The movement, led by Black Americans, for equal rights under the law. Jews were among those who came to join it.
Your line: justice for all. Three names, said together, the way they belong. See you tomorrow.

1034.title: War and peace
1034.hook: Israel's wars, and peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan
1034.howItsDone: The Amidah and the Kaddish end with a request for peace, and on Israel's Memorial Day for fallen soldiers, the day before Independence Day, sirens sound and people stand in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, civil rights, and your line: justice for all. Today, a harder subject: war, and the peace people made anyway.

An airplane door opens at an airport near Tel Aviv, at night. Down the steps comes the president of Egypt, Anwar Sadat, whose country had been at war with Israel. Israeli leaders wait at the bottom, some of them men who had fought against his army. Cameras flash. Reporters crowd the edge of the tarmac. Then hands are shaken. The next day he speaks to Israel's parliament in Jerusalem.
screen: `A PLANE DOOR OPENS.` → `THE PRESIDENT OF EGYPT.` → `HANDS ARE SHAKEN.`

segments.voice: Israel's story has included wars, and every war has had a cost on all sides: soldiers and civilians, parents who never got their children back. In Israel, the day for remembering fallen soldiers comes right before Independence Day, so grief and celebration stand next to each other. Peace came too, in pieces. After Sadat's visit, Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty, with Israel's prime minister Menachem Begin across the table. Years later, Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and King Hussein of Jordan made peace between their countries too. Peace with the Palestinians is still argued over, hoped for, and not yet reached. So what does the tradition say about peace? A psalm puts it in two verbs: "Depart from evil, and do good; Seek peace, and pursue it." An old midrash notices that other commandments wait for their moment: when you find a bird's nest, when you build a house. Peace you're told to seek and to chase. Hillel taught people to be like the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. And Isaiah saw a day when "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, And their spears into pruning-hooks." The swords aren't thrown away. They're reshaped into tools that grow food. The Amidah and the Kaddish both close with a request that the One who makes peace on high make peace for us. People who disagree fiercely about the wars can still say those words in the same room.
screen: `WARS, AND THEIR COST.` · `TREATIES WITH EGYPT AND JORDAN.` · `PEACE IS SOMETHING YOU CHASE.` · `SWORDS INTO PLOWSHARES.` · then, large: `SEEK PEACE, AND PURSUE IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where people are afraid tonight, a city, a border, a hospital, a home, and picture the people on every side of it, not as armies, but as families getting ready for bed. If you pray, use words that already exist, like the psalm's line: seek peace, and pursue it. If you don't, simply wish them a quiet night.

1035.title: Love and argument
1035.hook: Jews hold many views on Israel's politics; some love it, some criticize it, some do both
1035.howItsDone: Jews study Talmud in pairs, called chavruta, arguing over the text together, and the Mishnah's ideal of an argument 'for the sake of heaven' is often cited for disagreements in the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sadat, and your line: seek peace. Today, the argument that doesn't stop, and the love underneath it.

A Shabbat dinner table. The candles are lit, the bread is blessed, and somewhere around the soup someone mentions Israel's government. One cousin is furious at it. An uncle defends it, louder. A grandmother says she loves the country and is worried sick about it. Somebody's new partner, at the table for the first time, wonders whether to say anything at all. Nobody leaves. The arguing goes on through the chicken. Dessert still comes.
screen: `A SHABBAT TABLE.` → `A COUSIN, AN UNCLE, A GRANDMOTHER.` → `NOBODY LEAVES.`

segments.voice: Ask Jews about Israel's politics and you will hear many views. Some love the country and defend its choices. Some love it and criticize it hard. Some feel far from it. Some do several of these at once. Arguing hard is not new in this tradition. The Talmud is built out of disagreements, with the losing side's view kept on the page. The house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, two schools of rabbis, argued for years. The Talmud says a heavenly voice finally declared that both were the words of the living God, but the law would follow Hillel. Why Hillel? Because, the Talmud says, they were kind and humble, and they taught Shammai's view too, even putting it before their own. The Mishnah draws a line through all arguing: an argument for the sake of heaven will last; one that isn't, won't. Its good example: Hillel and Shammai. Its bad one: Korah and his followers, who argued with Moses to grab power. And the Torah puts love and honest challenge in a single verse. It begins, "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart," and in the same breath tells you to speak up when your neighbor does wrong. Read that way, criticism and love are not opposites, and keeping quiet can be a way of giving up on someone. The question is the Mishnah's: is this for the sake of heaven, to understand, or just to win? This lesson won't tell you what to think about Israel. It describes a very old way of arguing: loudly, honestly, at the same table, staying for dessert.
screen: `MANY VIEWS AT ONE TABLE.` · `THESE AND THESE ARE WORDS OF GOD.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.` · `LOVE AND REBUKE IN ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who sees something important very differently from you, in politics, faith or family, and picture them across a table. Let them speak first, and try to say their view back in a way they'd call fair, the way the house of Hillel taught the other side's words. You don't have to agree; just listen until you understand.
Hillel, whose school argued for years with Shammai's, and whose kindness and humility won the law's final word.

1036.title: Antisemitism today
1036.hook: old hatreds return, and communities answer with resilience
1036.howItsDone: At the Passover Seder, Jews sing that in every generation enemies rise up and God saves them, and today some synagogues keep holding services with security at the door and neighbors of other faiths invited in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel, and your line: love and argue. Today, a hard subject, and the courage that answers it.

On Yom Kippur, in the German city of Halle, a small congregation is praying through the long fast behind a heavy wooden door. Outside, a gunman tries to force his way in. He shoots at the door, again and again. The door holds. Unable to get in, he turns on people in the street nearby. And behind the door, the congregation keeps praying.
screen: `A WOODEN DOOR ON YOM KIPPUR.` → `THE DOOR HOLDS.` → `THE PRAYING GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Antisemitism is hatred of Jews for being Jews. It is old, and it keeps changing costumes: religious blame, racial theories, conspiracy stories about secret power or money, and sometimes anger at Israel that slides into blaming any Jew anywhere. In recent years it has come back in forms people had hoped were finished: attacks on synagogues in Pittsburgh and in Halle, graffiti on gravestones, harassment online and on the street, families wondering whether to wear a kippah or a Star of David in public. The Passover Haggadah has a line for this. It says that in every generation there are those who rise up to destroy the Jewish people, and that the Holy One saves them. Around the Seder table it's sung with cups raised, and then the meal goes on. The answer today looks like that. After the Pittsburgh attack, neighbors of many faiths came to stand in synagogues the next Shabbat, and Muslim groups raised money for the victims' families. Guards now stand outside some synagogues, and the services still happen. Children still go to Hebrew school. Doors still open. God's words to Joshua, before he leads the people across the Jordan, are a short command: "Be strong and of good courage." The verse goes on: don't be afraid or dismayed, for God is with you wherever you go. It's said at the riverbank, before the crossing, not after. This week walked from secret kitchens in Moscow to a zigzag on a bridge, from Heschel's praying legs to a Mississippi summer, from peace treaties to an argument at a Shabbat table. Each story had a hard thing in it, and someone who didn't step back.
screen: `AN OLD HATRED IN NEW COSTUMES.` · `IN EVERY GENERATION.` · `NEIGHBORS STAND IN THE PEWS.` · `DOORS STILL OPEN.` · then, large: `BE STRONG AND OF GOOD COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a Jewish friend, coworker or neighbor, or if none comes to mind, a synagogue or Jewish school near you and the people who walk through its doors, and hold them for a moment, by name if you can. Think of one simple message you could send, just thinking of you, presence rather than a speech; if you're Jewish yourself, you can let someone check on you, or reach out to someone else. If you pray, hold them in prayer.
Antisemitism today. Hatred of Jews returning in old and new forms, and communities who answer by keeping their doors open.
Your line: hate returns, courage too. Behind the door in Halle, the praying went on. That's day one thousand thirty-six.
